Physical product · Concept · 1 month

What if ironing felt as easy as using a mouse?

I set out to fix the ironing table and ended up redesigning the iron. Ergo Glider is a handle-free iron and steamer you hold the way you hold a computer mouse.

My process
The process

I got it wrong once before I got it right.

My first answer was a better ironing table. Peer feedback sent me back to the user journey, and the second time through I saw what I'd missed.

Ironing wasn't the problem. Setting up to iron was.

Eight steps, in the order I did them.

The project moved in two rounds of divergence and convergence. The first round found the right problem. The second found the right answer.

Step 1 of 8Desk research

The brief: make the bedroom work better.

I was asked to design a physical product that improves something people do in their bedroom. I didn't have an iron in mind, let alone a mouse. Desk research gave me four candidate routines: sitting up in bed, making one room do several jobs, keeping a wardrobe in order, and ironing. I wrote a problem card for each one.

Where I landed

Ironing came up in every set of interviews. Setting up to iron seemed tedious, so people skipped the board and ironed wherever they could.

These are the cards for the three routines I didn't pick. Each started with an idea I wanted to test, but people told me more than I asked about, and ironing kept coming up. So I narrowed down to ironing, and later to ironing on the bed. Click a card to read it.

Step 2 of 8User journey

I drew the morning before I asked about it.

To test the hunch, I sketched someone ironing a shirt before work. Then I mapped it into fourteen steps, each with an action, a thought and a feeling.

Step 3 of 8User interviews

Five conversations, and they all pointed at the bed.

After two interviews I refined my questions, then ran three more. Almost everyone ironed on the bed because that's where the plug point was. So I concluded that ironing on the bed was the problem.

{{ v }}
Step 4 of 8First concept

So I designed a table.

If the bed was the wrong surface, the answer seemed obvious: give people a better one. It looked like a storage cube most of the time and pulled out into an ironing table when needed. I built a working prototype. On paper, it ticked every box from the interviews:

  • →Height-adjustable for every body
  • →Quick to deploy, with storage for the iron
  • →Turns into regular furniture when not in use
Step 5 of 8Peer feedback

Then my peers reviewed it, and the table started to wobble.

What they said

There are already plenty of ironing tables on the market. A new one would still take up space, and folding and assembling it would still be a chore.

What it made me do

I'd redesigned the same problem in a different shape. So I went back to the journey and analysed it again, step by step.

Step 6 of 8Back to the journey

Ironing wasn't the problem. The setup was, whether it's a table or a bed.

Very few of the fourteen steps were actually ironing. The rest were setup: finding a plug, waiting for heat, bending over a surface, and leaving a hot iron to cool. A better table would only move that setup somewhere else.

  1. {{ j.a }} {{ j.tag }}
Step 7 of 8A new question

What if the bed was fine, and the iron needed to change?

People were going to iron on their beds anyway, so I stopped fighting that. I started exploring how to iron well on a soft surface, with nothing to set up and no cord. I started tracing over a regular iron, looking for the part the hand actually needs.

Step 8 of 8The idea

The palm already knows the perfect grip.

Traditional iron+Computer mouse=Ergo Glider

Most people spend hours a day with a hand resting on a mouse. I wanted that grip on the ironing board.

The product

Meet Ergo Glider.

A handle-free iron and steamer, shaped by the palm. There are no accessories to explain and nothing extra to remember.

Form

Five studies, one silhouette.

Once I knew it should be held like a mouse, I had to find the shape. These are the sketches, in the order I drew them.

Top view: from a leaf to an egg

I started with a long, narrow leaf shape. It was too thin for a palm. Widening the back turned it into an egg, which gave the hand somewhere to rest and the controls somewhere to live.

Side view: two shells and a ball

In side view I split the body into two shells, with a ball between them to carry pressure down to the soleplate. That became the pressure ball.

Under the palm

Then I worked out where the hand presses and how the thumb would reach the display, without letting go of the iron.
